items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's consider the graph of the function [MATH: f(x)=\sin x] and its tangent line [MATH: \color{orange}L] at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/179d445ecaf61334dcbb62da8b04012b]

Content:
From this graph, we see that near [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{3},] the tangent line and the function are very close to each other. So, the line [MATH: L(x)] is a good approximation of the function for points close to [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/790ee1ce583fc4db3fe1d4b9822716bf]

Content:
Here, the tangent line approximation of the function [MATH: f(x)=\sin x] at the point [MATH: a=\dfrac{\pi}{3}] is defined by
[MATH: L(x) = f\left( \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\left( x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right).]

Content:
Let's calculate [MATH: f\left( \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)] and [MATH: f' \left( \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)] in the expression above. Evaluating the function at [MATH: a=\dfrac{\pi}{3},] we get

Content:
[MATH: f\left( \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.]

Content:
and computing the derivative, we get
[MATH: f'(x)	=	\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\sin x)
=	\cos x,]
which in turn gives
[MATH: f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)	=	\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)
=	\dfrac{1}{2}.]

Content:
Finally, we obtain
[MATH: L(x)|= f((π)/(3)) + f^{′}((π)/(3))(x − (π)/(3)); = (sqrt(3))/(2) + (1)/(2)(x − (π)/(3)); = (sqrt(3))/(2) + (1)/(2)x − (π)/(6); = (1)/(2)x + (3sqrt(3) − π)/(6).]

sections.normalized_html: What is the tangent line approximation of [MATH: \tan x] at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}?]
sections.readable_text: What is the tangent line approximation of [MATH: \tan x] at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The tangent line approximation of [MATH: f(x) = \tan x] at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}] is [MATH: L(x) = f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) + f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\left( x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right).]

Let's compute [MATH: f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)] and [MATH: f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)] in the expression above. Evaluating the function at [MATH: a=\dfrac{\pi}{4},] we get [MATH: f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 1.]

Now, computing the derivative, we have [MATH: f'(x) = \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\tan x) = \sec^2 x,] which in turn gives [MATH: f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \sec^2 \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 2.]

So, the tangent line approximation is [MATH: L(x)|= f((π)/(4)) + f^{′}((π)/(4))(x − (π)/(4)); = 1 + 2(x − (π)/(4)); = 2x + 1 − (π)/(2).]

sections.normalized_html:
The tangent line approximation of [MATH: f(x)=\cos{x}] at the point [MATH: a=\dfrac{\pi}{2}] is [MATH: L(x) = f((π)/(2)) + f^{′}((π)/(2))(x − (π)/(2)).]

Let's compute [MATH: f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)] and [MATH: f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)] in the expression above. Evaluating the function at [MATH: a=\dfrac{\pi}{2},] we get

[MATH: f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \cos{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} =0.] Now, computing the derivative, we have [MATH: f^{′}(x)|= (d)/(dx)(\cos x) = − \sin x,] which in turn gives [MATH: f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\sin{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} = -1.]

So, the tangent line approximation is

[MATH: L(x)|= 0 − (x − (π)/(2)); = (π)/(2) − x.]

[MATH: \cos ((7π)/(12))|≈ L((7π)/(12)); = (π)/(2) − (7π)/(12); = − (π)/(12).]

sections.normalized_html: Approximate the value of [MATH: \cos{89^{\circ}}] using the tangent line approximation of [MATH: f(x) = \cos x] at [MATH: x=90^\circ.]
sections.readable_text: Approximate the value of [MATH: \cos{89^{\circ}}] using the tangent line approximation of [MATH: f(x) = \cos x] at [MATH: x=90^\circ.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Remember that the derivative of any trigonometric function is always expressed in radians. For that reason, we need to convert all degree units to radians.

To convert an angle expressed in degrees to an equivalent angle in radians, we multiply the angle in degrees by [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{180^\circ}.] This gives, [MATH: 90^\circ \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \dfrac{\pi}{2},] and [MATH: 89^\circ \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \dfrac{89\pi}{180} .]

The tangent line approximation of [MATH: f(x) = \cos x] at the point [MATH: a = 90^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{2}] is [MATH: L(x) = f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) +f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\left( x-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).]

Let's compute [MATH: f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)] and [MATH: f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)] in the expression above. Evaluating the function at [MATH: a = \dfrac{\pi}{2},] we get [MATH: f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0.]

Now, computing the derivative, we have [MATH: f'(x) = \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\cos x) = -\sin x,] which in turn gives [MATH: f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -1.]

So, the tangent line approximation is [MATH: L(x)|= 0 + (− 1)(x − (π)/(2)); = − (x − (π)/(2)); = (π)/(2) − x.]

We can approximate [MATH: \cos{89^{\circ}}] by evaluating the tangent line approximation at [MATH: a = 89^{\circ} = \dfrac{89\pi}{180}.] We get

[MATH: \cos 89^{∘}|≈ L((89π)/(180)); = (π)/(2) − (89π)/(180); = (π)/(180).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

From this graph, we see that near [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{3},] the tangent line and the function are very close to each other. So, the line [MATH: L(x)] is a good approximation of the function for points close to [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}.]

Content:
Here, the tangent line approximation of the function [MATH: f(x)=\sin x] at the point [MATH: a=\dfrac{\pi}{3}] is defined by
[MATH: L(x) = f\left( \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\left( x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right).]

Content:
Let's calculate [MATH: f\left( \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)] and [MATH: f' \left( \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)] in the expression above. Evaluating the function at [MATH: a=\dfrac{\pi}{3},] we get

Content:
[MATH: f\left( \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.]

Content:
and computing the derivative, we get
[MATH: f'(x)	=	\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\sin x)
=	\cos x,]
which in turn gives

Item 5 — Example: Computing the Tangent Line Approximation of a Trigonometric Function

Example Prompt:

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The tangent line approximation of [MATH: f(x) = \tan x] at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}] is
[MATH: L(x) = f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) + f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\left( x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right).]

Let's compute [MATH: f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)] and [MATH: f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)] in the expression above. Evaluating the function at [MATH: a=\dfrac{\pi}{4},] we get
[MATH: f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 1.]

Now, computing the derivative, we have
[MATH: f'(x) = \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\tan x) = \sec^2 x,]
which in turn gives
[MATH: f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \sec^2 \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 2.]

So, the tangent line approximation is
[MATH: L(x)|= f((π)/(4)) + f^{′}((π)/(4))(x − (π)/(4)); = 1 + 2(x − (π)/(4)); = 2x + 1 − (π)/(2).]
